original_value: Golf swing segmentation with inertial measurement units (IMUs) is an essential process for swing analysis using wearables. However, no attempt has been made to apply machine learning models to estimate and divide golf swing phases. In this study, we proposed and verified two methods using machine learning models to segment the full golf swing into five major phases, including before and after the swing, from every single IMU attached to a body part. Proposed bidirectional long short-term memory-based and convolutional neural network-based methods rely on characteristics that automatically learn time-series features, including sequential body motion during a golf swing. Nine professional and eleven skilled male golfers participated in the experiment to collect swing data for training and verifying the methods. We verified the proposed methods using leave-one-out cross-validation. The results revealed average segmentation errors of 5–92 ms from each IMU attached to the head, wrist, and waist, accurate compared to the heuristic method in this study. In addition, both proposed methods could segment all the swing phases using only the acceleration data, bringing advantage in terms of power consumption. This implies that swing-segmentation methods using machine learning could be applied to various motion-analysis environments by dividing motion phases with less restriction on IMU placement.

result.paraphrase: Golf swing segmentation using inertial measurement units (IMUs) is a key step for wearable-based swing analysis. Yet, machine learning models had not been used to estimate and partition golf swing phases. In this study, we proposed and validated two machine learning approaches that segment a complete golf swing into five main phases, including the pre- and post-swing periods, from each IMU attached to a body segment. The proposed bidirectional long short-term memory and convolutional neural network methods exploit automatically learned time-series features, including the sequential body movements during a golf swing. The experiment involved nine professional and eleven skilled male golfers, whose swing data were collected to train and evaluate the methods. We assessed the proposed methods with leave-one-out cross-validation. Results showed average segmentation errors of 5–92 ms for IMUs attached to the head, wrist, and waist, which were more accurate than the heuristic method used in this study. Moreover, both methods were able to segment all swing phases using only acceleration data, offering an advantage in power consumption. This suggests that machine learning-based swing segmentation can be applied in diverse motion-analysis settings by separating motion phases with fewer constraints on IMU placement.
